assessment.rationale: Good wire-level fit for sparse-knowledge, no-central-registry exchange of contested door-access evidence: [pcid,payload] is simple, canonical DAG-CBOR bytes aid stable hashing, and unknown pCIDs fail explicitly. But this is only an envelope specimen; membership, guest, override, revocation, freshness, and audit semantics remain outside the design, so local access decisions depend on additional wrapper and payload protocols.
strengths: Clear minimal boundary with explicit pCID dispatch and canonical DAG-CBOR encoding.
Unknown-pCID handling requires unsupported/unverified labeling, which helps safe salvage under partial knowledge.
Wrapper-based signatures/evidence can evolve without hard-coding a single central registry or fixed signing scheme.
weaknesses: Does not define the application objects and rules needed for membership, guest access, emergency override, or local promise accounting.
No fixed signature or audit slot makes consistent accountability depend on extra wrapper conventions.
Draft status and unminted pCID weaken present-day 100-year durability confidence.
risks: Operators or tooling may over-trust best-effort inspection of unknown payloads as authorization evidence.
Different wrapper conventions may produce inconsistent door decisions or audit trails across devices.
Fail-closed behavior on unknown or rotated pCIDs could cause lockouts during migration or partitions.
open_questions: Which pCIDs and payload schemas represent grants, revocations, guest passes, and emergency overrides?
What local deny/degrade/escalate policy should a door controller use when wrappers, handlers, or freshness proofs are missing or stale?
How are replay protection and door-event audit records linked when signatures live only in wrapper protocols?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.
